extracted.intended_audience: aspiring poets, dramatists, and students of poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing poetic works and stage plays (poetry, tragic and satyric drama) with attention to plot, metre, chorus, style, revision, and publication. Emphasises classical/Horatian standards of verisimilitude, brevity, workmanship, and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not stage graphic impossible acts; narrate them
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid showing onstage what must be narrated to be credible: 'so that Medea is not to butcher her boys before the people, nor impious Atreus cook human flesh upon the stage, nor Procne be turned into a bird, Cadmus into a snake.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violent or fantastical deeds that strain credibility should be conveyed by an actor's telling or by implication (eyes/facundia) rather than enacted literally. The audience should be shown only what they can reasonably accept onstage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit play length to five acts if revival is desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Let no play be either shorter or longer than five acts, 'if when once seen it hopes to be called for and brought back to the stage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain conventional structural length (five acts) to increase chances of repeat performance and audience acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid deus ex machina except for truly worthy knots
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let a god intervene unless 'a knot come worthy of such a deliverer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rescue devices (divine intervention) must be justified by the plot's gravity; avoid arbitrary contrivances that undercut causal integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit speaking characters (max three actors on stage)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Nor let a fourth actor essay to speak’ — i.e., not more than three speaking characters should be on stage at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the number of speaking roles manageable for clarity and tradition; avoid overcomplicating scenes with too many simultaneous speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must advance plot and embody moral standpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Let the Chorus sustain the part and strenuous duty of an actor, and sing nothing between acts which does not advance and fitly blend into the plot. It should side with the good and give friendly counsel… praise wholesome justice, law, and peace… keep secrets, and pray and beseech the gods…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus as an active, coherent dramatic force: only include choral material that contributes to plot, tone, or moral perspective; avoid irrelevant lyrical digressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep musical accompaniment simple and supportive
rubrics_metrics.description: The flute should be 'slight and simple, with few stops' and serve to lead and aid the chorus rather than rival trumpets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instrumentation should support speech and choral song; avoid flashy or dominating musical elements that distract from drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain dignity when shifting between tragic and satyric modes
rubrics_metrics.description: When passing from grave to gay (e.g., tragedy to satyr play), 'no god, no hero… shall shift with vulgar speech into dingy hovels,' and tragedy should not be turned into trivial verses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transitions across registers/styles must preserve the essential dignity of characters recently seen in elevated guise; avoid jarring shifts that collapse register or character status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve character-appropriate voice (forest creatures vs city folk)
rubrics_metrics.description: When Fauns or satyr-figures come from the forest, 'they should... beware of behaving as though born at the crossways and almost as dwelling in the Forum' — do not give them city or forum-like speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that characters' diction and behaviour align with their origins and social type; avoid inconsistent or anachronistic voices (mawkish verses or coarse jokes in inappropriate characters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order and connexion (sequence/juncture) are vital
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Such is the power of order and connexion, such the beauty that may crown the commonplace.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong sequence and structural linkage can elevate otherwise ordinary material; prioritize coherent plotting and logical progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate life and manners as models for characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn to real life and manners for a model: 'the drama is an imitation of life… give each character his fitting part.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study human relations, social roles, and duties so characters act plausibly within their roles (parent, friend, judge, general, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Study exemplars (Greek models) thoroughly and constantly
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Handle Greek models by night, handle them by day’ — study exemplar books repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classical models to learn form, rhythm, and diction; sustained, repeated study refines taste and technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice craft and revise repeatedly; labour refines poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Many days and many blots have 'restrained and refined ten times' — the poet must sweat, toil, and repeatedly correct to achieve excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polish through extensive revision and critical refining; do not expect raw talent alone to produce finished work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and art must conjoin — talent needs training
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither study without natural vein nor native wit untrained will suffice: 'each claims the other's aid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate innate talent with disciplined study, practice, and abstention from distractions; both are necessary for durable quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be brief and avoid the superfluous when instructing
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Whatever you teach, be brief, so that what is quickly said the mind may readily grasp… every superfluous thing flows away from a full mind.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor concise exposition and economy of language when aiming to instruct; trim excess that dilutes impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictions should be near the truth (verisimilitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Fictions meant to please should be close to the real, so that your play must not ask for belief in anything it chooses.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain plausibility in invented elements; do not ask audiences to accept implausible events without preparation or justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix profit and pleasure — combine instruction and delight
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Omne tulit punctum qui miscuit utile dulci’ — the work that blends useful and sweet wins the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for works that both instruct (moral/utile) and entertain (dulce); this maximizes audience impact and longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow occasional faults but avoid repeating the same error
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poem has many beauties, Horace will pardon a few blots caused by carelessness or human frailty; but a scribe or player who repeats the same fault lacks excuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor imperfections are tolerable in otherwise strong works; habitual, repeated mistakes (same flaw) are unforgivable — fix recurring faults through discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish hastily; conceal or destroy immature works
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a critic (Maecius), father's ear and Horace's own judge hear it, then 'put your parchment in the closet and keep it back till the ninth year… delere licebit quod non edideris; nescit vox missa reverti.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay publication for prolonged self-critique and external judgement; unpublished work may be destroyed; once public, words cannot be recalled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid relying on flatterers; seek genuine critical judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not bring a delighted gift-recipient to hear verses, for friends will cry 'Pulchre! Bene! Recte!' — flattery misleads; hired mockers can move more than sincere admirers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test work with impartial critics, not only with friends or paid applauders; beware of biased praise that conceals defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend to metre and lawful rhythm; learn ear and finger
rubrics_metrics.description: Study lawful rhythm: 'with fingers and ear can catch the lawful rhythm' — be able to distinguish coarseness from wit and proper measures (e.g., iambic trimeter usage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master metric conventions and rhythmic propriety; meter matters to musicality and public taste (e.g., acceptance of spondees in certain positions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be content with mediocrity; aim for merit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediocre poets are not tolerated ('mediocribus esse poetis non homines, non di, non concessere column ae'); poems that fall short sink to the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for excellence; half-measures or indifferent craft will be scorned by discerning audiences and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt style to audience distance: some works need close inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Ut pictura poesis: erit quae, si propius stes, te capiat magis, et quaedam, si longius abstes.’ — some poems please on close scrutiny, others at a distance; some please once, others repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different pieces require different modes of reception: adjust clarity, obscurity, and density according to intended audience and purpose.
